title: The Letter to the Romans
subtitle: Pros Rhōmaious, “To the Romans”
description: Paul’s longest letter, written to a church he had never visited, and the fullest account he ever gave of the gospel he preached: “I am not ashamed of the gospel.” Every human being, Jew and Gentile alike, has sinned; God declares the ungodly righteous as a free gift, through faith, as he did Abraham; Adam’s trespass is answered by Christ’s obedience; and for those in Christ Jesus there is no sentence of condemnation, and nothing in all creation can cut them off from God’s love. Then Israel and the nations, bodies offered as a living sacrifice, a church of the strong and the weak learning to welcome one another, and a long list of friends to greet. The letter that turned Augustine, Luther and Wesley. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Romans?
qa.answer: The sixth book of the New Testament and the longest of the apostle Paul’s letters, written to the Christians in Rome. It sets out the gospel more fully than anything else Paul wrote: that all have sinned, that God declares people righteous as a free gift through faith in Jesus Christ, that those in Christ live by the Spirit, that God has not abandoned Israel, and that a people shown such mercy must live by love. Its theme is stated in 1:16–17, the gospel as God’s power to save everyone who believes.

qa.question: Who wrote Romans, and when and where was it written?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, who names himself in the first verse. He dictated it to a secretary, Tertius, who adds his own greeting (16:22). It was almost certainly written from Corinth, around AD 57, near the end of Paul’s work in the eastern Mediterranean, as he was about to take a gift from the Gentile churches to Jerusalem. It was probably carried to Rome by Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae, Corinth’s port, whom Paul commends in 16:1–2.

qa.question: Why did Paul write to the Romans?
qa.answer: Paul had never been to Rome, and he planned to visit on his way to preach in Spain, hoping the Roman church would pray for him and help him on (15:22–33). The letter introduces him and the gospel he preaches. It also speaks to a church of Jewish and Gentile believers who did not always agree, about food, holy days and their standing before God, and urges them to welcome one another as Christ has welcomed them (15:7).

qa.question: What does “justification by faith” mean in Romans?
qa.answer: The Greek word translated “justify”, which this translation renders “declare righteous”, is a law-court word for a judge’s verdict that someone is in the right. Paul teaches that God gives this verdict to the guilty not because of their works but as a free gift, received by trusting him, on the ground of Christ’s death (3:21–26). Abraham is his example: he “believed God, and that was counted to him as righteousness” (4:3). Christians differ on how this verdict relates to the new life that follows, and recent scholars have debated what Paul meant by “works of the law”, but all agree it is God’s gift and not a human achievement.

qa.question: What is Romans 9–11 about?
qa.answer: God’s faithfulness to Israel. If most of Paul’s own people have not believed in their Messiah, has God’s word failed? Paul answers that God has always worked by choosing and by mercy, that there is a remnant of Israel chosen by grace, that Gentile believers are like wild branches grafted into Israel’s olive tree, and that “all Israel will be saved” (11:26). Christians read these chapters differently, especially on election and on what “all Israel” means, but Paul ends them in worship of a God whose ways are past tracing out (11:33–36).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
